summary: Describes the relational extension to Sieve, which lets tests use relational operators and test counts of entities in header and envelope fields as well as their content. It replaces RFC 3431. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: Sieve is a small language that mail servers run to sort mail into folders. Its basic tests only ask whether a header equals a given text. This document adds two more kinds of test: one that compares a value against another, and one that counts how many addresses or headers a message has.

questions: what is the sieve relational extension
sieve value vs count match type
subtitle: Teaching a mail filter to compare values and count the entries in a header.

tldr.problem: The base Sieve language can only test whether a header or address matches a string. It cannot ask whether a value is bigger than another, or how many addresses a message has.
tldr.mechanism: The RELATIONAL extension adds two match types, :value and :count, that take one of six operators (gt, ge, lt, le, eq, ne). :value compares strings; :count compares the number of entities with a number.
tldr.outcome: A filter can now do things like file mail with an X-Priority below 3 into a Priority folder, or flag mail with more than 5 recipients. It is a Proposed Standard that replaces RFC 3431.

facts.value: gt, ge, lt, le, eq, ne

today: RFC 5231 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2008. It obsoletes RFC 3431 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard way to compare and count values in a Sieve script.

sections.title: What the Extension Adds
sections.content:
The RELATIONAL extension to the Sieve mail filtering language provides relational operators on the address, envelope and header tests. It also provides a way of counting the entities in a message header or address field.

With this extension a Sieve script can determine whether a field is greater than or less than a value instead of just equivalent. One use is the x-priority field: move messages with a priority greater than 3 to the "work on later" folder. Mail could also be sorted by the from address, with those userids that start with 'a' to 'm' going to one folder and the rest to another.

The script can also determine the number of fields in the header, or the number of addresses in a recipient field, for example whether there are more than 5 addresses in the to and cc fields.

The capability string associated with the extension is relational.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail servers can already file mail away using a small script language called Sieve. This document lets those scripts ask new kinds of question, such as whether a priority number is above 3, or whether the message went to more than five people.

sections.title: Comparators
sections.content:
This document does not define any comparators and does not exempt any comparators from the require clause. Any comparator used must be treated as defined in the Sieve specification.

The i;ascii-numeric comparator, as defined in RFC 4790, MUST be supported for any implementation of this extension. That comparator MUST support at least 32-bit unsigned integers. Larger integers MAY be supported. The comparator does not support negative numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: A comparator decides how two pieces of text are compared, for example ignoring case. The extension insists on one comparator that compares numbers, and it must handle unsigned 32-bit numbers at least.

sections.title: The Syntax and the Six Operators
sections.content:
The document defines two new match types, the VALUE match type and the COUNT match type. Their syntax is:

MATCH-TYPE =/ COUNT / VALUE

COUNT = ":count" relational-match

VALUE = ":value" relational-match

relational-match = DQUOTE
        ("gt" / "ge" / "lt" / "le" / "eq" / "ne") DQUOTE

The six operators are "gt" for greater than, the C operator ">", "ge" for greater than or equal, ">=", "lt" for less than, "<", "le" for less than or equal, "<=", "eq" for equal to, "==", and "ne" for not equal to, "!=".

The VALUE match type does a relational comparison between strings. It may be used with any comparator that returns sort information. A value taken from the message is the left side of the relation, and a value from the test expression, the key-list for the address, envelope and header tests, is the right side. If there are multiple values on either side, or on both sides, the test is true if any pair of values satisfies the relation.
sections.plainLanguage: Each new test names one of six comparisons: greater than, greater or equal, less than, less or equal, equal, and not equal. The value from the message is always on the left and the value written in the script on the right, and the test passes if any one pair matches.

sections.title: What the COUNT Match Type Counts
sections.content:
The COUNT match type first determines the number of the specified entities in the message, then does a relational comparison of that number to the values specified in the test expression. It SHOULD only be used with numeric comparators.

The Address Test counts the number of addresses, that is the number of mailbox elements as defined in RFC 2822, in the specified fields. Group names are ignored, but the mailboxes they contain are counted.

The Envelope Test counts the number of addresses in the specified envelope parts. The envelope "to" will always have only one entry, the address of the user for whom the Sieve script is running, so using this test there is no way to tell whether the message was actually sent to someone else. The envelope "from" will be 0 if the MAIL FROM is empty, or 1 if MAIL FROM is not empty.

The Header Test counts the total number of instances of the specified fields. It does not count individual addresses in the "to", "cc" and other recipient fields.

In all cases, if more than one field name is specified, the counts for all specified fields are added together to obtain the number for comparison. Specifying ["to", "cc"] in an address COUNT test therefore compares the total number of to and cc addresses; if separate counts are wanted, they must be done in two comparisons, perhaps joined by "allof" or "anyof".
sections.plainLanguage: The count test answers a different question for each kind of test. For addresses it counts the mailboxes. For the envelope it counts the addresses the message was sent from and to. For a header it counts how many times the header appears, not how many addresses are inside it.

sections.title: Interaction with Other Sieve Actions
sections.content:
This specification adds two match types. The VALUE match type only works with comparators that return sort information, and the COUNT match type only makes sense with numeric comparators.

There is no interaction with any other Sieve operations, nor with any known extensions. In particular, this specification has no effect on implicit KEEP, nor on any explicit message actions.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding these tests does not change what any other part of a Sieve script does. A message that is filed away is still kept, and a message a script discards is still discarded.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
Given a message with two received headers, a subject of example, a to field of two addresses and a cc field of one address, the test address :count "ge" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["to", "cc"] ["3"] evaluates to true, because the counts are added together and reach three. The test anyof ( address :count "ge" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["to"] ["3"], address :count "ge" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["cc"] ["3"] ) evaluates to false, because neither field on its own reaches three.

To check the number of received fields in the header, the test header :count "ge" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["received"] ["3"] evaluates to false for that message, but header :count "ge" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["received", "subject"] ["3"] evaluates to true, because the subject is counted as well.

The test header :count "ge" :comparator "i;ascii-numeric" ["to", "cc"] ["3"] always evaluates to false on an RFC 2822 compliant message, since a message can have at most one to field and at most one cc field. That test counts the number of fields, not the number of addresses.

The extended example in Section 7 shows the extension used together. A script that requires the relational capability and the numeric comparator files mail with an x-priority below 3 into a Priority folder, treats a to field with more than 5 recipients as SPAM, splits the rest by the first letter of the from address, and files mail addressed only to the user into a separate folder.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show the difference between counting fields and counting addresses. Two to addresses and one cc address make three addresses, but only two header fields. The script at the end of the section puts those ideas together into a filter that sorts mail into four folders.

sections.title: Changes since RFC 3431
sections.content:
Apart from several minor editorial and wording changes, the notable changes since RFC 3431 are the following. The references were updated, including changing the comparator reference from the Application Configuration Access Protocol to the Internet Application Protocol Collation Registry, RFC 4790. The examples were updated and corrected. Definition comments were added to the ABNF for "gt", "lt" and the other operators. The document clarified which RFC 2822 elements are counted in the COUNT test. And the requirement to strip white space from header fields before comparing was removed, because a more general version of that requirement has been added to the Sieve base specification.

The extension is registered with IANA under the capability name relational, described as extending existing conditional tests in the Sieve language to allow relational operators.
sections.plainLanguage: The new document keeps the same extension and the same capability name as the one it replaces. The changes are small: better examples, clearer wording about what gets counted, and a reference to the current registry of text comparison rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: An implementation MUST ensure that the test for the envelope "to" only reflects the delivery to the current user. Using this test, it MUST not be possible for a user to determine whether the message was delivered to someone else. Additional security considerations are discussed in the Sieve specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A filter script must not be able to work out whether the message was also sent to other people. The envelope to field always shows only the address of the user running the script, so nothing else is revealed.
